title: Choose a Deployment Shape and Operating Model
summary: Choose among workstation, container, on-premises, edge, and cloud shapes from workload evidence, data boundaries, ownership, and recovery needs.
objectives: Translate a model-serving idea into a bounded workload, service objective, data boundary, and failure budget.
Compare workstation, container, on-premises, edge, and cloud deployment shapes without assuming one is inherently private, cheap, or reliable.
Assign identity, security, platform, model, data, evaluation, capacity, incident, and recovery ownership.
Select a reversible initial shape with explicit evidence, constraints, review triggers, and an exit path.

paragraphs: Write the users, tasks, model class, input and output modalities, sensitivity, concurrency, arrival pattern, context size, output length, latency objective, availability target, geographic boundary, disconnected requirement, retention rule, and recovery objective. sections.title: Compare five useful deployment shapes
paragraphs: A workstation can support individual learning, offline experiments, and low-concurrency development, but user sessions, sleep, local privilege, thermal limits, and unmanaged changes make it a weak default for a shared service. A container adds a reproducible process boundary and packaging contract; it does not by itself add strong isolation, authentication, backups, high availability, or resource limits. In production environments, engineers must account for token utilization patterns, context window pressure, and deterministic execution boundaries. When system constraints or rate limits are approached, explicit retry strategies with exponential backoff and jitter prevent cascading failures across downstream dependencies.

On-premises infrastructure can align with local data, connectivity, and hardware-control requirements while transferring capacity, patching, power, cooling, spare-parts, and incident ownership to the operator. Edge deployments reduce distance or support intermittent connectivity but constrain power, memory, update bandwidth, physical security, and repair. In production environments, engineers must account for token utilization patterns, context window pressure, and deterministic execution boundaries. When system constraints or rate limits are approached, explicit retry strategies with exponential backoff and jitter prevent cascading failures across downstream dependencies.

Cloud compute can provide faster provisioning, managed infrastructure options, and elastic capacity, but it still requires verified region, identity, networking, encryption, quotas, cost controls, observability, backup, and exit planning. Hybrid designs add routing and consistency choices. None of these labels proves privacy, cost efficiency, performance, or resilience. In production environments, engineers must account for token utilization patterns, context window pressure, and deterministic execution boundaries. Do not claim high availability because multiple replicas exist on one host or because an orchestrator can restart a broken process. sections.title: Assign operating ownership before deployment
paragraphs: Name accountable owners for model and license review, artifact integrity, host and accelerator lifecycle, runtime, identity and access, secrets, network policy, data handling, evaluation, capacity, cost, telemetry, vulnerability response, abuse handling, incident command, backup, restore, rollback, and end-of-life. activity.title: Create a deployment-shape decision record
instructions: Define one synthetic workload with users, data class, request distribution, context and output sizes, latency and availability objectives, disconnected needs, and recovery objectives.
Score workstation, containerized single host, on-premises service, edge appliance, cloud service, and one hybrid option against the same criteria.
Draw the process, host, site, identity, network, storage, registry, and management-plane failure domains.
Assign all operating roles and identify every role without a qualified owner.
Choose a bounded first shape, define stop and migration triggers, and write how to return to a known safe state.
evidence: A dated workload and service contract with normal and failure behavior.
A comparable shape matrix, failure-domain map, and ownership matrix.
A reversible decision record with rejected alternatives, stop conditions, migration path, and review triggers.

instructorScript.transcript: Define users, data, demand, latency, availability, disconnection, retention, and recovery before naming a platform. Describe normal requests and what must happen when the service is slow, unavailable, overloaded, wrong, or unsafe. Explain that workstation, container, on-premises, edge, cloud, and hybrid labels do not prove privacy, cost, performance, or resilience. A workstation may fit individual experiments; a container improves packaging but does not create authentication, resource limits, backup, or availability; on-premises, edge, and cloud each transfer different responsibilities rather than removing them. Separate process, host, accelerator, storage, network, identity, scheduler, site, registry, and management-plane failures. Test the failure domain actually claimed. Assign accountable owners for every control, lifecycle, evidence, incident, and recovery responsibility. Record authority, escalation, evidence, and substitutes. Choose the smallest reversible deployment that can safely prove the next operational claim. Preserve rejected alternatives, stop conditions, a migration path, and triggers that force the decision to be reviewed again.

questions.prompt: What should be defined before choosing hardware or cloud services?
choices: Users, workload, data, demand, service objectives, failures, and recovery
questions.explanation: The service and failure contract determines what infrastructure evidence is relevant.

questions.prompt: What does putting a model server in a container establish by itself?
choices: Reproducible packaging and a process boundary, subject to the actual configuration
questions.explanation: Containers help package and bound processes but do not automatically provide the other controls.

questions.prompt: Why are two replicas on one host insufficient evidence for host availability?
choices: Both replicas share the same host failure domain
questions.explanation: Redundancy inside a shared failure domain does not survive loss of that domain.

questions.prompt: Which statement about local deployment is accurate?
choices: It changes the control and operating boundary but still requires verified privacy, security, cost, and recovery
questions.explanation: Locality is a design fact, not proof of every desired property.

questions.prompt: What makes an ownership assignment operationally useful?
choices: Authority, evidence, escalation, on-call expectation, and a substitute
questions.explanation: Ownership must connect responsibility to authority, evidence, availability, and escalation.

questions.prompt: What is the safest first deployment shape?
choices: The smallest reversible shape that safely proves the next claim
questions.explanation: A bounded reversible step produces decision evidence without unnecessary operational scope.
